body: Somebody carried the harmonium round from two streets away. For the second day of a wedding the front room has been cleared of everything except chairs and that. An aunt is playing it badly and knows she is playing it badly. The tabla player is a cousin who does weddings and funerals and nothing in between. Somebody props an exercise book against the harmonium, the soft kind with a grid on the cover, and the singing starts from that. It is full of hymns in Bengali in a grandmother’s handwriting, copied and translated by her over about forty years, in two colours of ink because at some point one pen ran out. Three people know the tunes. The rest follow a line behind.

That exercise book is not a keepsake and it is not a craft project. It is the distribution system. For a great many Bengali-speaking Christians it is the whole of the distribution system, and when the grandmother dies it goes into a drawer.

Bengali is among the most spoken languages on earth. It has a literary tradition of the first rank, a Nobel laureate poet whose songs are still sung daily, and a musical culture in which words and melody are unusually tightly bound. Christian radio in it is close to absent.

Absent is the precise word, and it is worth separating from the words people reach for instead. Not banned. Not suppressed. Not censored, not fought over, not lost in a fire. Simply never made — a different condition, and in some ways a more embarrassing one, because there is nobody to blame and therefore nothing to overturn. A thing that was never made has only an absence where a decision would have been, and absences do not appear in anybody’s minutes. Nobody decided Bengali did not matter. It simply never cleared a commercial threshold, which produced the same result.

So the frequency was assigned before the audio existed. HM 333.80 — Bengal Inspire — is assigned and in build, and it is not yet on air; nothing plays there today. The number is held for it on a dial running from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 that currently carries 121 stations.

Assigning a number to a station that cannot yet be heard is an odd thing to do, and it is the most expensive decision on this band. A held frequency earns nothing. It cannot be given to a station with a bigger audience while it waits, it cannot be quietly dropped if the catalogue takes longer than expected, and it sits on the dial as a standing promise somebody will have to keep. That is the point of doing it in public. A gap with a number on it is much harder to leave alone than a gap that is merely regrettable.

It is worth being specific about why gaps like this last for generations, because the reason is boring and that is what makes it durable. Producing a catalogue in a language requires either a market that can fund it or a donor base that already cares about it. Bengali-speaking Christians are a minority within a population that is itself not a wealthy media market, so the first route does not open. And a donor base cares about what it has heard of, which means the second route depends on somebody having already managed the first. Every step of that chain is about money and none of it is about need. The chain has never been unfair to anybody in particular, and it has produced an unfair result for a very long time.

The band is arranged to break that chain rather than to argue with it. Each language holds one permanent frequency, hosted in the language rather than dubbed into it, sitting in an international block beside its regional neighbours. There is no drive-time slot to be won, no schedule to be competed for, and no editorial meeting where a language has to justify its share of an hour. The frequency is either assigned or it is not, and once assigned it does not get taken back.
Which changes the question being asked, and the change is the argument.

The commercial question is a reasonable question, asked in good faith by serious people. Can this be afforded? Will it return what it costs? Is there a cheaper way to reach these listeners — a shared regional station, an hour on a Sunday, a subtitled version of something that already exists? Each of those is a sensible answer to the question as posed, and each ends in the same place: the language gets a fraction, and a fraction is what the grandmother with the exercise book was already providing on her own. The question is not wrong. It is simply not about the listener at all, and after enough decades of asking it, nobody notices that.
Remove the licensing cost, collapse the production cost, and the question changes by itself.

In a hospice in Birmingham an old woman is sitting with her husband in the late afternoon while the ward does its four o’clock things around them. She has run out of anything to say and she does not want the television. The night nurse, who is Filipina and has been on this ward for six years, puts something on quietly from her own phone on the windowsill — HM 339.90, the Tagalog station, because it is what she has on. The old woman does not understand a syllable of it. After a while she notices the nurse humming along while she writes on the chart, and asks what the song is, and the nurse says it is about the Lord being her strength, and goes back to the chart. The old woman would rather it were in Bengali. It is not. She leaves it on for two hours.

That is the mechanism the argument turns on, and it works in both directions at once. It worked for the nurse because her language has a frequency. It worked for the old woman because somebody left a language she did not speak playing in the room.

The honest part is that this article cannot end with the Bengali station. It is not on air. There is no catalogue behind it yet, a catalogue takes musicians and rooms and time, and until that work is done the frequency is a number and a commitment and nothing you can put on this afternoon. The gap is still there. What has changed is that it now has a number on it.

But the reason to say that plainly is that the argument does not need the pretence. If the case for a Bengali station only worked once the station existed, it would not be a case at all — it would be a description. The case is that the gap was indefensible on the day the frequency was assigned, with no audio behind it whatsoever, and that a gap being indefensible is by itself sufficient reason to hold a number open. That is the opposite of a commercial threshold, and it is the only mechanism that has ever got a small language onto a dial.

So the Bengali station is not evidence of anything yet. It is a receipt. It says that at least once, somebody looked at a language with an enormous number of speakers and almost nothing on the air in it, and treated the absence as a fault to be fixed rather than as a market conclusion to be respected.
All of which is a promise until something is actually playing. So here is something that is.

The dial carries four kinds of programming, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of the band — worship, gospel, hymns, country and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to leave running in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards, with more frequencies assigned and still in build behind the ones already on air.

If you want to hear what the Bengali station will be, listen to HM 339.90 — Pilipinas Inspire, the Tagalog station, which is on air now. It is the same decision, already carried out. Tagalog would not clear a commercial threshold in any Western media market either, and there it is, running day and night with its own presenters and its own catalogue, hosted rather than dubbed. Put it on for an hour and you are not sampling a foreign format. You are listening to the evidence that a frequency held open for a language with no obvious business case eventually turns into music coming out of a speaker, which is the only argument this article actually has.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which languages people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next frequency gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a campaign. Put HM 339.90 on this evening in a room where somebody else can hear it, and if they ask what it is, say it is a station in a language that nobody was ever going to fund. That sentence is the whole of it. And if Bengali is your language, or your mother’s, the number is already on the dial with your name against it — which is not the same as music, and is a great deal more than an exercise book in a drawer.
